interest: This file offers an immediate, contemporary window into the rapid evolution of Canadian wartime policy toward Japanese Canadians during the pivotal six weeks between the attack on Pearl Harbor and the mid-January 1942 announcements that preceded total coastal expulsion. It documents the critical intelligence liaison between American diplomats in Vancouver, the U.S. Legation in Ottawa, and U.S. intelligence agencies (FBI, MID, ONI), highlighting how Canadian policies on demographic registration, fishing fleet immobilization, and coastal 'protected areas' were studied by U.S. authorities as they formulated their own Japanese exclusion policies culminating in Executive Order 9066. Additionally, the candid observations of Consul General Josselyn provide valuable social and political history, recording early predatory economic pressures on Japanese property owners, anti-Japanese political lobbying from British Columbia municipalities, and the domestic political maneuvering of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF).
overview: This file (decimal file 894.20242H, File 1324), spanning December 1941 to January 1942, comprises diplomatic despatches, inter-agency transmittal memoranda, and contemporary newspaper clippings regarding the surveillance, demographic breakdown, property control, and impending removal of persons of Japanese ancestry in British Columbia following the outbreak of war between Canada and Japan. Authored primarily by Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General in Vancouver, and addressed to the Secretary of State and American Minister Pierrepont Moffat in Ottawa, the documents record early wartime security measures enacted under the Defense of Canada Regulations. These include the RCMP's detailed registration of 23,428 Japanese residents, the closure of Japanese-language schools and newspapers, the impoundment and proposed liquidation of approximately 1,100 Japanese-operated fishing boats, the restriction and surveillance of the Japanese Consulate staff in Vancouver, and the comprehensive national policy statement issued by Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King on January 14, 1942, establishing coastal protected areas, civilian labor corps, and strict prohibitions on Japanese economic and navigational activities.

subfiles.about: Covering despatch transmitting copies of a report sent to the U.S. Legation in Ottawa regarding Japanese in British Columbia.
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Paul R. Josselyn in Vancouver transmits to Secretary of State Cordell Hull five copies of his confidential despatch of the same date sent to the U.S. Legation at Ottawa regarding the Japanese situation in British Columbia. The cover despatch bears Department of State processing stamps indicating receipt on December 18, 1941, and referral to the Division of European Affairs. It officially places the consular report into the State Department's central decimal filing system under 894.20242H/2.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 986 from Josselyn (Vancouver) transmitting report on Japanese in British Columbia

subfiles.about: Consular report detailing demographic statistics, police surveillance, school closures, boat impoundment, and security measures regarding Japanese in British Columbia immediately after Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.summary: Consul General Josselyn provides Minister Pierrepont Moffat with an initial survey of the 23,428 Japanese residents in British Columbia following the outbreak of hostilities between Canada and Japan. The despatch includes a complete statistical tabulation from the RCMP's summer 1941 registration categorized by gender, marital status, and citizenship (Canadian-born, naturalized, Japanese nationals, and U.S. citizens). Josselyn reports on the detention of fewer than 30 suspected individuals, the closure of three Japanese newspapers and all language schools, the impoundment and disabling of roughly 1,000 fishing boats, and the police surveillance placed on Japanese Consul Ichiro Kawasaki, while expressing his own skepticism regarding public resolutions of loyalty from Canadian-Japanese organizations.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Josselyn (Vancouver) to Moffat (Ottawa) on Japanese in British Columbia

subfiles.about: Department of State memorandum circulating Consul General Josselyn's report to American military, naval, and federal intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State formally transmits copies of strictly confidential Despatch No. 986 (cited with a clerical error as No. 906) from Vancouver to the Military Intelligence Division (MID), the Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). The memorandum reflects the immediate distribution of diplomatic intelligence regarding foreign Japanese populations to U.S. defense and security branches following Pearl Harbor. It is marked with departmental filing symbols FW894.20242H/2.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum transmitting Vancouver despatch to U.S. intelligence agencies
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Federal Bureau of Investigation

subfiles.about: Covering despatch transmitting two follow-up reports sent to the U.S. Legation in Ottawa regarding developments affecting Japanese in British Columbia.
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.summary: Consul General Josselyn forwards to the Secretary of State five copies each of his despatches to the U.S. Legation in Ottawa dated January 16 and January 21, 1942. These reports record significant policy decisions reached by the Canadian federal government concerning the evacuation and control of Japanese residents. The transmittal is recorded under file number 800 and received departmental file classification 894.20242H/3.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1049 from Josselyn (Vancouver) transmitting further reports to Washington

subfiles.about: Diplomatic letter reviewing the Ottawa conference on Oriental affairs, coastal protected areas, fishing vessel liquidation, property disposal pressures, and British Columbia legislative politics.
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.summary: Consul General Josselyn summarizes discussions between Dominion officials and British Columbia delegates, including Mayor F. J. Hume and Provincial Labor Minister George S. Pearson, leading to the federal decision to exclude enemy aliens from coastal 'protected areas.' He outlines plans to employ adult male aliens in work corps, details the creation of a three-man committee (Justice Sidney Smith, Commander B. L. Johnson, and Kishizo Kimura) to sell or charter 1,100 impounded fishing vessels, and relays concerns from Custodian of Enemy Property agent G. W. MacPherson regarding predatory purchases of Japanese property. The report also highlights resistance in the Okanagan Valley to permanent Japanese resettlement, notes the arrival of U.S. Army intelligence officers in Vancouver, quotes provincial military enlistment figures, and analyzes the socialist wartime platform of CCF opposition leader Harold Winch in the provincial legislature.
subfiles.title: Letter from Josselyn (Vancouver) to Moffat (Ottawa) on Japanese removal policy and provincial politics

subfiles.about: Covering despatch transmitting the published text of Canadian Prime Minister Mackenzie King's formal statement on Japanese restrictions.
subfiles.from: Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General, Vancouver
subfiles.summary: Consul General Josselyn transmits to American Minister Moffat in Ottawa the printed text of the official statement issued by Canadian Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King on January 14, 1942. The despatch notes that the text appeared in the Vancouver press on the same day and confirms that five copies are simultaneously transmitted to the Department of State in Washington. It serves as the official diplomatic record for the enclosed press clipping.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Josselyn (Vancouver) to Moffat (Ottawa) transmitting Prime Minister King's statement

subfiles.about: Newspaper text of Prime Minister Mackenzie King's comprehensive policy statement detailing security restrictions, vessel immobilization, coastal exclusion, and labor corps for Japanese in Canada.
subfiles.from: W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada (via Canadian Press)
subfiles.summary: The Vancouver Daily Province reproduces the complete statement released by Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King outlining the Canadian Dominion Government's policies regarding persons of Japanese racial origin and other enemy aliens. The statement announces the total prohibition of Japanese from commercial fishing, the controlled sale of gasoline and explosives, bans on short-wave radios and cameras for Japanese nationals, and the mandatory removal of enemy aliens without police permits from newly defined coastal protected areas. It also details the formation of a civilian corps for Canadian-Japanese volunteers, promises protection for law-abiding Japanese and their property, notes special consideration for Japanese Canadian World War I veterans, and lists the members of the Standing Committee on Orientals chaired by Mayor Fred J. Hume.
subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping from The Vancouver Daily Province: Text of Prime Minister King's statement
